IACC SUMMARY OF ADVANCES IN AUTISM RESEARCH
The Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC) is a federal advisory committee charged with coordinating 
federal activities concerning autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and providing advice to the Secretary of Health and 
Human Services (HHS) on issues related to autism. The Committee was established by Congress under the Children's 
Health Act of 2000, reconstituted under the Combating Autism Act of 2006, and renewed most recently under the 
Autism Collaboration, Accountability, Research, Education, and Support (CARES) Act of 2019.
Membership of the Committee includes a wide array of federal agencies involved in autism research and services, 
as well as public stakeholders, including autistic adults, family members of those on the autism spectrum, advocates, 
service providers, and researchers, who represent a variety of perspectives. The IACC membership is composed 
to ensure that the Committee is equipped to address the broad range of issues and challenges experienced by 
individuals and families in the autism community. 
Under past and present authorizing legislation, the IACC was and is currently required to (1) develop and annually 
update a strategic plan for autism research, (2) develop and annually update a summary of advances in autism 
research, and (3) monitor federal activities related to autism.
Through these and other activities, the IACC provides guidance to HHS and partners with other federal departments, 
research and advocacy organizations, and the broader autism community to accelerate research and enhance 
services with the goal of positively impacting the lives of people on the autism spectrum and their families.

INTRODUCTION
THE 2023 IACC SUMMARY OF ADVANCES 
IN AUTISM RESEARCH
Each year, the IACC releases a list of scientific advances that represent significant progress in the field of autism 
research. The Summary of Advances provides short, lay-friendly summaries of the top research breakthroughs 
selected by the IACC from a pool of research articles nominated by the members. The 20 studies selected for 
2023 provide new insight into racial and ethnic disparities in autism services, timing of early intervention services, 
and trajectories of co-occurring health conditions across the lifespan. The advances also include studies that 
investigated novel screening and diagnostic tools, explored developmental trajectories, and updated prevalence 
estimates for autism in children. Articles in the Summary of Advances are grouped according to the topics 
represented by the seven Questions of the IACC Strategic Plan. Citations for the articles selected for the Summary 
of Advances, as well as a complete listing of those nominated, are included at the end of the document. 
Editorial Note on References to Autism: The IACC supports the use of accessible language around autism  
in its publications. The terms "person with autism," "person with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)," "autistic person," 
and "person on the autism spectrum" are used interchangeably throughout this document. Some members of the 
autism community prefer one term, while others prefer another. The Committee respects the different opinions within 
the community on the use of this language and does not intend to endorse any particular preference. In addition, 
the term "autism" is generally used in this document, and “ASD” is used when referring specifically to the DSM-5-TR 
defined diagnosis.

Differential Performance of Social Communication Questionnaire Items in African 
American/Black Vs. White Children. 
Dahl E, Moody EJ, Barger B, Rosenberg S, DiGuiseppi C, Fallin MD, Lee LC, Wiggins L. J Autism Dev Disord. 
2023 Mar 10.  [Read Abstract Here]
SCREENING AND DIAGNOSIS
At-a-Glance:
Differences in how Black and White children respond to the Social Communication 
Questionnaire (SCQ) can lead to unequal accuracy of results that may reinforce 
racial inequalities.
Background: The estimated prevalence of autism is similar among Black and White children. However, studies have 
found continuing racial inequities in age of diagnosis, service use, and quality of care. One potential reason for these 
inequities may be that the tools used to screen for ASD perform differently based on race and ethnicity. Studies 
have found that several commonly used screening tools, such as the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ), 
do not produce equally accurate results across different demographic groups. Individuals in different racial and 
ethnic groups may show differential item response patterns (i.e., different groups understand and respond to the 
same question differently based on personal experience). To evaluate these patterns, the investigators performed 
a statistical analysis of “Differential Item Functioning” (DIF) from a large, diverse sample of preschool children with 
autism. 
Methods & Findings: Researchers analyzed responses from 3,376 participants to the SCQ screening tool for ASD, 
which asks caregivers to respond to questions related to characteristics of autism (e.g., inconsistent eye contact, 
minimal use of gestures). The data was taken from the Study to Explore Early Development (SEED), which has 
collected data from a large, diverse sample of children with autism. Researchers then used DIF analyses to identify 
consistent differences in responses for Black and White children. The analysis showed that 41% of the SCQ items 
performed differently across Black respondents and White respondents. These results suggest that performance on 
the SCQ may not be similar for Black and White children. These differences in responses to the SCQ could result in 
both over-representing and under-representing autism characteristics in these populations and could contribute 
to racial disparities in identification of autism.

SCREENING AND DIAGNOSIS
Implications: The findings suggest that clinicians should be aware of performance differences when using the 
SCQ to decide whether to refer a Black child for evaluation for autism. ASD diagnostic tools that do not account 
for differences in children’s backgrounds may perpetuate disparities in the availability and timing of an ASD 
diagnosis, which in turn delays referral for early intervention services and supports. These findings are particularly 
important because the SCQ is likely to be used at ages when Black children are typically screened for ASD (older 
than 30 months). Further research is needed to understand how and why screening tools perform differently across 
racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic groups. One possibility is that sociodemographic differences, such as education 
level, cultural differences, or regional context, could contribute to differing interpretations of certain screening 
questions. To develop and adapt ASD screening tools that are culturally appropriate and equally valid among 
people with diverse backgrounds, assessments could potentially revise the wording of some questions, remove or 
add certain items, or use unique cutoff scores for different groups.

Predictive Value of Early Autism Detection Models Based on Electronic Health 
Record Data Collected Before Age 1 Year. 
Engelhard MM, Henao R, Berchuck SI, Chen J, Eichner B, Herkert D, Kollins SH, Olson A, Perrin EM, Rogers U, 
Sullivan C, Zhu Y, Sapiro G, Dawson G. JAMA Netw Open. 2023 Feb 1;6(2):e2254303. [Read Abstract Here]  
[Free Full Text Article]
At-a-Glance:
Data from electronic health records can be used to help detect autism in 
children by 1 year of age, complementing other screening methods. 
Background: Early detection of autism in childhood enables access to supportive resources and interventions, 
which improve outcomes. However, many autistic children are identified too late to fully benefit from early support. 
The most commonly used early autism screening tools are recommended between 16 to 30 months of age, but 
detection of very early signs might help to reach a diagnosis at even younger ages. A promising approach to 
early autism detection consists of passively monitoring electronic health records (EHR) using prediction models 
for autism-correlated characteristics (i.e., using a computer algorithm to detect characteristics in the health 
records), such as low birth weight, premature birth, respiratory infections, or difficulty sleeping or feeding. This 
study examined whether computer algorithm-mediated analysis of EHR data could be used to help detect autism 
as early as 30 days after birth.
Methods & Findings: The data included in this study drew from more than 14 years of EHR data from 45,080 
children. The EHRs reflected a population that was racially, ethnically, and socioeconomically diverse. EHRs came 
from children who met the criteria for autism, ADHD, and other neurodevelopmental conditions, as diagnosed by 
clinicians prior to the study, as well as from typically developing children with no diagnoses who were included as 
a control group. Analysis of diagnostic codes found that 924 (1.5%) of children in the sample met autism criteria. 
Multiple EHR variables were analyzed using a computer algorithm to predict autism diagnosis. Children’s prior 
diagnoses, medications, procedures, demographics, vital signs, outpatient and inpatient encounters, and laboratory 
findings were shown to be reliable predictors of an autism diagnosis. The algorithm-based prediction model was 
able to identify nearly half (45.5%) of autistic children in the dataset at 30 days after birth, and over half (59.8%) 
by age one, while limiting false positive rates (i.e., the percentage of times a test incorrectly identifies something 
as present when it isn't) to 10.0% and 18.5%, respectively. Notably, the model was also able to detect autism in 
children with co-occurring ADHD or other neurodevelopmental conditions, which can be associated with delayed 
autism diagnosis. Additional analyses showed that good performance of the model was not limited to particular 
demographic groups.

Implications: This study found that EHR data from the first year of life can be used to reliably predict future 
autism diagnosis. Results suggest that EHR-based monitoring could be integrated with existing screening tools 
and caregiver surveys to improve the accuracy of early autism screening. In contrast with existing screening tools, 
EHR-based autism detection can occur at a much earlier age (30 days) and may help to avoid late autism diagnosis, 
especially in children with co-occurring ADHD or other neurodevelopmental conditions. Another positive of this 
method is that it is passive and does not require any additional data collection. Further work should be done to 
expand upon the potential benefits of EHR-based detection of autism.

SCREENING AND DIAGNOSIS
At-a-Glance:
Eye-tracking technology, which tracks where children look during social 
interactions, can reliably identify autism in children between 16 and 
30 months old.
Background: Many parents report noticing signs of developmental issues by a child’s second birthday, but the 
average age of ASD diagnosis is much later, around 4 to 5 years of age. This means that for many families, access to 
supportive services may be delayed. Prior research has shown that social visual engagement (i.e., how children look 
at and learn from the social environment) is a promising potential measure of autism. This study and the companion 
article linked above developed and replicated a new eye-tracking test intended to aid early autism diagnosis and 
assessment in children aged 16 to 30 months, when characteristic traits of autism may begin to be noticeable.
Methods & Findings: These studies evaluated the accuracy of an eye-tracking measure of social visual engagement 
in predicting ASD diagnosis made by expert clinicians using standardized assessments. Participants included more 
than 1,500 children aged 16 to 30 months who were assessed for autism. Participants watched videos of social 
interactions while eye-tracking data were collected to measure presence or absence of autism as well as to assess 
children’s individual levels of social disability, verbal ability, and nonverbal cognitive ability. The results were then 
compared with expert clinical ASD diagnosis to determine the eye-tracking test’s diagnostic accuracy. Across both 
studies, results showed that the eye-tracking test matched expert clinicians in 84% of cases. The eye-tracking test 
results also correlated with clinical assessments of individual levels of social skills, verbal ability, and nonverbal 
cognitive ability. Further, the eye-tracking test performed similarly across all racial and ethnic groups in the studies.
Implications: The results of these studies indicate that eye-tracking measurement of social visual engagement 
can be a valid, objective indicator that can reliably identify autism and thus facilitate early ASD diagnosis. This 
evidence led to the FDA clearance of this as the first objective test to aid in the diagnosis and assessment of autism 
in 16-30-month-old children. Standardized ASD assessments often require hours of testing and may be skewed by 
participant and clinician bias. In contrast, objective measurements of child behavior, together with automated data 
collection and analysis, as evaluated in these studies, can generate objective data and diagnostic results within 30 
minutes. Given these promising findings, evaluation of this performance-based eye tracking measure as an early 
autism identification tool in routine specialty clinical practice is warranted.

At-a-Glance:
A tablet-based digital app that captures behavioral signs of autism can be used 
to improve screening of children from diverse populations in non-research 
settings, complementing other screening methods.
Background: Autism screenings are commonly conducted during primary care visits for children between 18 and 
24 months of age. However, studies have demonstrated that some autism screening questionnaires have lower 
accuracy in real-world healthcare settings (e.g., primary care) than in research settings, particularly for children 
from racial and ethnic minority populations and girls. Research has demonstrated that eye-tracking is a reliable 
measure of social attention and may aid in the detection of autism, but there are not comparable measures of 
behavior that can reliably assess other characteristics of autism (e.g., restricted and repetitive behaviors and social 
communication abilities). Digitally capturing multiple behaviors—such as gaze patterns, head movements and facial 
expressions—and then analyzing the behaviors in a process called digital phenotyping could help to provide a fuller 
picture. To this end, researchers developed and tested the SenseToKnow application (app), which displays short 
videos on a tablet device and records and analyzes a child’s behavioral responses to the videos.
Methods & Findings: Participants included 475 children aged 17 to 36 months, 49 of whom were diagnosed 
with autism and 98 of whom were diagnosed with a developmental delay. Researchers used the SenseToKnow 
app to assess participants during primary care wellness visits. The SenseToKnow videos were designed to elicit 
characteristic autism-related behaviors, including differences in social and attention indicators, facial expressions, 
head movement frequency and complexity, blink rate, motor behaviors, and children’s responses to their own 
names. As the children watched the videos on the tablet, the app used computer vision and machine learning 
to capture and analyze the children’s behavioral responses to the videos. SenseToKnow was able to accurately 
distinguish between children with autism, children with a developmental delay, and neurotypical children. 
Researchers confirmed SenseToKnow’s diagnostic accuracy by following up with participants up to age four years 
old. The app’s performance was largely consistent across race, ethnicity, and sex.
Early Detection of Autism Using Digital Behavioral Phenotyping.
Perochon S, Di Martino JM, Carpenter KLH, Compton S, Davis N, Eichner B, Espinosa S, Franz L,  
Krishnappa Babu PR, Sapiro G, Dawson G. Nat Med. 2023 Oct;29(10):2489-2497. [Read Abstract Here]

Implications: These findings highlight the benefits of comprehensive autism screening practices that incorporate 
multiple methods, which can include questionnaire-based assessments and digital-based behavioral observation, 
among other screening methods. This study’s results are strengthened by its diverse sample, real-world design 
(i.e., it was conducted during regular wellness visits), and confirmation of autism diagnosis after the study. 
SenseToKnow’s reliability across different demographics indicates that it could be helpful in reducing autism 
diagnostic disparities that affect historically underrepresented populations. Future studies of SenseToKnow can 
further examine children of varying ages and language abilities.

BIOLOGY
At-a-Glance:
Key behavioral features of autistic people may be explained by differences 
in the strength of connections between brain regions and the activity of 
certain genes.
Background: While difficulties with verbal communication, social interaction, and repetitive behaviors are key 
features of autism, not all autistic people experience these to the same extent, and no two autistic individuals are 
alike. Research has shown that the strength of connections between brain regions (known as “functional networks”) 
differ between autistic and neurotypical people. Differences among these functional networks may also explain 
variation in behaviors among autistic people. In addition, these functional networks are managed by the activity 
(or “expression”) of different genes, which could also play a role in individual experiences of autism. This study 
examined functional networks and patterns of gene expression that are associated with different behaviors in 
people with autism. 
Methods & Findings: Researchers used brain activity and behavioral data from 299 autistic and 907 neurotypical 
people to identify differences in brain functional networks that contribute to verbal, social, and repetitive and 
restrictive behaviors (RRBs). They identified four different groups of autistic people who were characterized by 
different traits: one group had high verbal IQ, one had low verbal IQ, one had more social challenges but fewer RRBs, 
and one had fewer social challenges but more RRBs. Each of these groups was associated with distinct patterns of 
functional connectivity across various brain regions, especially regions involved in emotion/stress response, sensory 
and motor function, and the default mode network (which becomes active when a person’s mind is wandering 
and not focused on the outside world). The researchers then identified specific genes that were associated with 
each group’s behaviors and affected brain functional networks. For example, the functional network of the group 
with more RRBs was associated with decreased expression of HTR1A, a gene involved in serotonin signaling (i.e., a 
chemical “messenger” that affects mood and many other body functions). Previous work has also found this gene 
to be associated with RRBs in people with autism.
Implications: This study identified differences in brain connectivity and gene expression that may contribute to 
key features of autism and found that these can vary greatly from one autistic individual to the next. These findings 
provide new information on what brain, genetic, and other biological changes may affect autistic people’s behaviors, 
in particular verbal communication, social challenges, and RRBs. This improved understanding could help to develop

therapy services than those without ID, only 15% of those with ID received mental health services compared to 34%

non-autistic individuals of the same age and sex. Researchers found that 8% of autistic females had at least one

Background: The transition to adult health care can be challenging for autistic individuals, particularly because 
autistic people tend to have more co-occurring health conditions than the general population. However, only a small 
number of studies have evaluated how co-occurring health conditions may change over time in autistic adolescents. 
Prior studies have evaluated prescription medication use but not specific physical or mental health diagnoses. This 
study analyzed the trajectory of common physical and mental health conditions in autistic adolescents as they 
enter adulthood.
Methods & Findings: Using data maintained by Kaiser Permanente Northern California for 1,418 autistic and 
6,029 non-autistic adolescents (ages 14 to 17 years in 2014), researchers examined electronic medical records 
from 2014 to 2019 to identify physical and mental health conditions that commonly co-occur in autistic adolescents 
and adults. Researchers found that, compared to non-autistic adolescents, autistic adolescents of all ages 
experienced higher prevalence of obesity, epilepsy/seizures and other neurological disorders, sleep difficulties, 
anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder (ADHD), and depression. Additionally, autistic adolescents had 
higher prevalence of dyslipidemia (i.e., abnormally high or low lipid levels in the blood), but prevalence of other 
cardiovascular diseases was similar for autistic and non-autistic adolescents. Although the prevalence of all physical 
and mental health conditions increased with age for both autistic and non-autistic adolescents, the prevalence of 
obesity and dyslipidemia increased at a faster rate among autistic adolescents. When comparing differences by sex, 
researchers found that autistic females experienced a higher prevalence of all medical and psychiatric conditions 
compared to autistic males by age 22.  
Implications: Findings from this study indicate that autistic adolescents, particularly autistic female adolescents, 
experience higher prevalence of many common co-occurring physical and mental health conditions as they age into 
adulthood. These findings highlight the need for interventions including routine screening and health education 
to improve health outcomes for autistic adolescents. Future studies are needed to determine what factors may be 
contributing to the development of co-occurring conditions to identify prevention strategies. Additionally, work 
is needed to evaluate trends in co-occurring health conditions into older adulthood and among individuals with 
co-occurring intellectual disability to better understand the intervention and services needs of autistic individuals 
across the lifespan.

data from 2020 estimates that 1 in 36 8-year-old children in the United States

Background: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities 
Monitoring (ADDM) Network collects data on autism and other developmental disabilities in children living in the 
United States. ADDM Network data has been used by the CDC, community members, lawmakers, and researchers 
to track trends in autism prevalence across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic groups.  ADDM data can inform efforts 
to increase equitable access to services and support for all children with autism. This study focuses on the ADDM 
Network’s monitoring of autism prevalence among 8-year-old children in 2020.
Methods & Findings: In 2020, across 11 ADDM Network sites, approximately 1 in 36 8-year-old children had autism 
documented in their medical or educational records. Prevalence of autism among boys was 4.3%, 3.8 times higher 
than prevalence among girls (1.14%). Autism prevalence was lower in White children (2.43%) and children of two or 
more races (2.29%) than in Black (2.93%), Hispanic (3.16%), and Asian/Pacific Islander children (3.34%). Although 
lower autism prevalence was associated with higher median household income at three sites (Arizona, New Jersey, 
and Utah), no association was found between autism prevalence and income at the other eight sites. Among the 
66.7% of autistic children whose cognitive abilities were documented, 37.9% were classified as having an intellectual 
disability (ID). Autistic girls were more likely to have co-occurring ID compared to autistic boys (42.1% vs 36.9%), 
and Black autistic children were more likely to have co-occurring ID than White autistic children (50.8% vs 31.8%). 
Among children with recorded evaluations, almost half (49%) of autistic children were evaluated by the time they 
were 3 years old, and the median age of first diagnosis was 49 months. Further, autistic children with ID were 
diagnosed at a median age of 43 months, while autistic children without ID were diagnosed at a median age of 
53 months.
